actionThatDiffers: Read the blocked question off the board and either type the answer immediately or consciously defer it, instead of walking every pane to discover which one is asking and what it asks.
why: Briefing: a session state is fully visible in its own pane, and needs-input detection exists only for Claude. A capture-pane sweep dumps the visible prompt text from every pane in one pass, which is an adequate approximation of what each is waiting for, so access sits mid-scale rather than high. Split assumed: reliable blocked-state detection is Claude-only; on the other nine harnesses the user reads raw pane text and infers. dependsOnDetector true because the state badge rests on a heuristic reading of the transcript tail. Impact is real but bounded: answering still requires going to the pane, so what changes is triage order and pre-composed answers, not the work itself.

actionThatDiffers: Jump straight into the right pane from the board rather than cycling terminal tabs to find which one is which.
why: Rule 5: this is something the user does, not information. Today it is a tmux window switch or a terminal tab click - one move in a place the user already knows, so 21-40. With 3-12 tabs the hunt costs seconds, not minutes. Impact is mild convenience: the action taken afterwards is identical, only the seconds of tab-scanning differ, so it stays under 50 per rule 1.

actionThatDiffers: Go back to a finished worktree and commit, push or open the PR - or delete the branch - instead of leaving the work stranded until it is discovered weeks later or lost to a cleanup.
why: git status and gh pr list are each one command, but the item is about sessions that have already ended, so the pane sweep in rule 2 does not reach them: you must first know which repos and worktrees agents touched, then check each. Briefing is explicit that no harness retains queryable cross-session history, so this is correlating across sessions and time - the 61-80 band. It is not unobtainable, hence not above 80. Impact is the highest of my nine because the loss is concrete and permanent: uncommitted agent work in a forgotten worktree, or a PR that never got opened.

actionThatDiffers: On returning, open the one session that needs a decision and act on it, instead of scrolling three to twelve scrollbacks to find out which ones moved.
why: The raw material is on disk and in scrollback, so it is reachable, but assembling a digest means reading every output for the away period - capture-pane gives only the visible tail, not what scrolled past. No harness retains queryable history (briefing), so this is correlating across sessions and time. dependsOnDetector true: a digest is a judgement about what mattered, not a revealed field, so its value rests on that judgement being right. Impact held under 60 because the follow-up action is the same work the user would have done after reading; what changes is the minutes of re-reading, and a wrong digest can hide the item that mattered.

actionThatDiffers: Answer a hosted or cowork session that is blocked in the same triage pass as the local ones, rather than remembering to go check a browser tab separately.
why: The briefing does not cover cloud, cowork or hosted sessions at all, so this is first-principles and marked low. Reasoning: a hosted session lives in a web UI the user already has open and already knows to look at, which is one click in a known place - 21-40. What is missing is co-location with the local board, not the data. Impact is moderate: the same answering action happens either way, and the loss avoided is a delay in noticing, not lost work. Split assumed: applies only to the harnesses that actually have a hosted or cowork surface, which is a minority of the ten.

actionThatDiffers: none - the item itself records no decision attached, and I could not name one; a version string does not change what the user does next.
why: Access is low: each CLI answers --version in one command in a place the user knows, and a handful of harnesses means a handful of commands, still inside 21-40 for the ones that matter at any moment. Health is visible from whether the process is alive (ps) and whether the pane is printing. Impact is near the floor by rule 1: the outcome field says no decision attached, and I can name no action that differs. Interesting, not actionable.

actionThatDiffers: Start the next task on the machine or teammate box that is idle, or stop duplicating work a teammate already has an agent on - rather than piling everything onto the box in front of you.
why: Briefing is silent on multi-machine and team, so low confidence. Nothing native crosses a machine boundary: the pane sweep in rule 2 stops at the host. A second machine needs an SSH session plus the same sweep repeated, and a teammate needs asking them - effectively unobtainable by hand for the team case, so 81-100. Impact is held mid-scale for the modelled user, who is one developer with terminal tabs: the rebalancing decision is real but occasional, and it is a coordination convenience rather than prevention of concrete loss.

actionThatDiffers: Close or restart the sessions that went quiet, reclaiming the tab and catching one that died or has been waiting unnoticed - instead of leaving them to accumulate.
why: Rule 3 applies: this is a threshold over per-session last-activity, and the input is approximable by a sweep - tmux list-panes exposes pane activity and ps shows liveness, so a six-line loop yields an adequate approximation, capping access at 60. I set 50 rather than lower because no harness shows idle duration on screen. Rule 6: scored as if unshipped. dependsOnDetector true because the two-hour cut and what counts as activity are heuristic choices, not revealed data. Impact is a real recurring decision but the loss avoided is attention and tab clutter, not work.

actionThatDiffers: Leave the machine or start a second task for a bounded stretch instead of babysitting the pane, and come back at the estimate rather than checking every ninety seconds.
why: Elapsed time for the current turn is on screen in the pane, but the briefing states flatly that no harness estimates how long a turn will take, and no third-party tool listed computes it. So the ETA half does not exist anywhere: rule 4 puts access high and forces dependsOnDetector true, because the value rests entirely on the estimator being accurate. I held it at 78 rather than 90 because the elapsed input, which is half the item, is directly visible. Impact is a real recurring decision - wait, switch, or intervene - but capped below 76 because a noisy ETA on agent turns changes timing rather than preventing loss, and the 15-minute overrun warning is where the loss-prevention actually lives.
